title: DocOps: Benchmarking Agents That Edit Real Documents
hook: Even frontier agents can't reliably edit complex documents: a verifiable benchmark pins the failures on three modes — state-tracking collapse, shallow verification, and destructive metadata edits.
key_points: DocOps deterministically verifies document-operation tasks via a taxonomy of atomic operations stacked into escalating workflow complexities.
Across many agent harnesses, even top closed- and open-source models fail on highly coupled, long-range document tasks.
Failure mode 1: long-term state tracking collapses over multi-step edits.
Failure mode 2: verification stays shallow — agents confirm surface text, not true semantic correctness.
Failure mode 3: agents destructively edit structural metadata, breaking global document consistency.
content_html: In a July 2026 paper, Jiang and colleagues introduce DocOps, a benchmark for autonomous agents that manipulate real digital documents — the spreadsheets, slides, and files that fill everyday workspaces. Its tasks are deterministically verifiable: a hierarchical taxonomy breaks document work into atomic operations and stacks them into progressively harder, multi-step workflows. Testing leading closed- and open-source models across several agent harnesses, the authors find that even the strongest frontier setups struggle badly once tasks become long and tightly coupled.
extra_html:
Where agents break

The authors report three recurring failure modes. Agents suffer long-term state-tracking collapse, losing the thread of what they've already changed over a long edit. Their verification is shallow — they confirm that surface text looks right rather than checking whether the document is actually correct. And they perform destructive edits to structural metadata, quietly breaking the scaffolding that keeps a document internally consistent.

Why it matters

Reliable document editing is a prerequisite for general-purpose AI assistants that automate office work, and DocOps argues today's agents aren't there yet: they can't maintain global consistency across a complex document. The authors frame this as a call for more robust, non-destructive agent designs, and offer a verifiable yardstick to track progress. As with related computer-use benchmarks, the bottleneck is less about low-level control and more about planning, memory, and verification over long horizons.
